General Mills, Inc. (NYSE: GIS) today announced the pricing terms, expiration and results of its previously announced tender offers (each, a “Tender Offer” and together, the “Tender Offers”) to purchase for cash the debt securities issued by General Mills referred to below (collectively, the “Notes,” and each a “Series”).

Each Tender Offer has been made upon the terms and subject to the conditions set forth in the Offer to Purchase dated October 5, 2026 (the “Offer to Purchase”) and any related documents (together with the Offer to Purchase, the “Tender Offer Documents”). Capitalized terms used but not defined in this press release have the meanings given to them in the Offer to Purchase.

The Tender Offers expired at 5:00 p.m., New York City time, on October 9, 2026 (such time and date, the “Expiration Date”). Withdrawal rights for the Tender Offers expired at the Expiration Date, and accordingly, Notes validly tendered in the Tender Offers may no longer be withdrawn except where additional withdrawal rights are required by law.

Monday 10/12

Fixed-income markets are closed in observance of Columbus Day.

Tuesday 10/13

Third-quarter earnings season commences, with financials leading the way. Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs Group, and Wells Fargo release quarterly results on Tuesday, followed by Bank of America, BlackRock, and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday, and Charles Schwab and Interactive Brokers Group on Thursday. Outside of financials, Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth Group announce earnings on Tuesday.

Wednesday 10/14

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the consumer price index for September. Consensus estimate is for a 3.6% year-over-year increase, two-tenths of a percentage point more than in August. The core CPI is expected to rise 2.5% from 2.4% previously.

Thursday 10/15

The Census Bureau reports retail sales data for September. Economists forecast a 0.3% month-over-month gain, after a 1.1% jump in August. Excluding autos and gas, sales are seen rising 0.2%.

data.title: Limestone Custom Homes: New Colorado ADU Law Makes 2026-2027 the Right Time for Douglas County Homeowners to Build an Accessory Dwelling Unit
data.description:
Limestone Custom Homes: New Colorado ADU Law Makes 2026-2027 the Right Time for Douglas County Homeowners to Build an Accessory Dwelling Unit

Limestone Custom Homes: New Colorado ADU Law Makes 2026-2027 the Right Time for Douglas County Homeowners to Build an Accessory Dwelling Unit

PR Newswire

CASTLE ROCK, Colo., Oct. 9, 2026

State law HB24-1152 removes long-standing barriers for homeowners in Castle Rock, Parker, Highlands Ranch, and Lone Tree

CASTLE ROCK, Colo., Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Limestone Custom Homes, a Castle Rock-based design-build custom home company, today said the 2026-2027 building season is shaping up as the most favorable window in recent memory for Douglas County homeowners to build an accessory dwelling unit (ADU). Colorado's HB24-1152, which took effect June 30, 2025, now requires communities including Castle Rock, Parker, Lone Tree, and unincorporated Douglas County to allow one ADU on single-family lots through an administrative approval process, replacing a patchwork of local rules that discouraged many homeowners from moving forward.

Under the new law, qualifying jurisdictions can no longer require additional off-street parking for an ADU in most cases, impose owner-occupancy requirements, or apply stricter design standards to an ADU than to the main home. The law also voids HOA covenants that prohibit ADUs outright, a significant change in HOA-heavy Douglas County, though associations may still apply reasonable design standards.

According to Limestone Custom Homes, Douglas County homeowners pursuing ADUs are typically motivated by a few consistent goals: housing for aging parents or adult children, long-term rental income to offset rising housing costs, home offices and studios, and guest suites. Many plan for more than one, designing a unit for a family member today that can become a rental later.

"Douglas County homeowners have wanted to build ADUs for years. The demand was always there, and the process was the obstacle," a Limestone Custom Homes spokesperson said. "With administrative approval now the standard, homeowners who had shelved ADU plans are taking a second look. Whether it's a detached backyard cottage, a garage conversion, or a finished basement with a separate entrance, the path is much clearer than it was two years ago."

As an ADU builder in Colorado, Limestone designs and builds accessory dwelling units throughout Douglas County and the Denver metro area, managing architecture, permitting, construction, and finish selections with one in-house team from its Castle Rock office.

About Limestone Custom Homes

Limestone Custom Homes is one of Colorado's leading design-build custom home companies, with offices in Castle Rock and projects across Douglas County, the Denver metro area, the Colorado mountains, and Larimer County. The company specializes in high-end custom homes and ADUs with a fully in-house design, architecture, and construction team. For more information, visit Limestone Custom Homes.

data.title: Microvast Investigation Continued: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Continues to Investigate the Officers and Directors of Microvast Holdings, Inc. - MVST
data.description:
Microvast Investigation Continued: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Continues to Investigate the Officers and Directors of Microvast Holdings, Inc. - MVST

Microvast Investigation Continued: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Continues to Investigate the Officers and Directors of Microvast Holdings, Inc. - MVST

PR Newswire

NEW YORK and NEW ORLEANS, Oct. 9, 2026

NEW YORK and NEW ORLEANS, Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Former Attorney General of Louisiana, Charles C. Foti, Jr., Esq., a partner at the law firm of Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC ("KSF"), announces that KSF has continued its investigation into Microvast Holdings, Inc. (NasdaqCM: MVST).

On November 21, 2023, J Capital Research published a report entitled "MVST: Empty Facilities and a Grant Loss That Was Probably Hidden: Another China Hustle" alleging that the Company knew that a proposed $200 million U.S. Department of Energy Grant to help fund a proposed polyaramid separator production facility had been rescinded for months prior to a May 2023 Reuters report, but failed to inform investors. The report further alleged that "the majority of MVST's sales may be fake"; that "Chinese customers account for 57% of revenue in 2023" but drone footage showed the Company's Chinese factory "shows almost no activity"; that the Company "has disappeared from Chinese procurement lists" and "local competitors say the company is not making discernible sales," and that the Company's reported backlog was "dubious."

Thereafter, the Company and certain of its executives were sued in a securities class action lawsuit, charging them with failing to disclose material information in violation of federal securities laws. The court presiding over that case has denied the Company's motion to dismiss in part, allowing the case to move forward. 

KSF's investigation is focusing on whether Microvast's officers and/or directors breached their fiduciary duties to its shareholders or otherwise violated state or federal laws. 

If you have information that would assist KSF in its investigation, or have been a long-term holder of Microvast shares and would like to discuss your legal rights, you may, without obligation or cost to you, call toll-free at 1-833-538-3606 or email KSF Managing Partner Lewis Kahn (lewis.kahn@ksfcounsel.com), or visit https://www.ksfcounsel.com/cases/nasdaqcm-mvst/ to learn more.

data.title: Catholic Charities USA launches relief fund for those impacted by Hurricane Isaias
data.description:
Catholic Charities USA launches relief fund for those impacted by Hurricane Isaias

Catholic Charities USA launches relief fund for those impacted by Hurricane Isaias

PR Newswire

ALEXANDRIA, Va., Oct. 9, 2026

ALEXANDRIA, Va., Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As forecasters warn that Hurricane Isaias will bring devastating winds and dangerous storm surges to the Gulf Coast, Catholic Charities USA (CCUSA), the official domestic relief agency of the Catholic Church in the United States, has launched a dedicated disaster relief donation campaign (ccusa.online/isaias). One hundred percent of all funds raised will be allocated to local Catholic Charities agencies, which will provide critical relief — including shelter, food and other humanitarian aid — to displaced and suffering members of their communities.

"Our sisters and brothers along the Gulf Coast need our prayers and support as this powerful storm threatens their communities," CCUSA President and CEO Kerry Alys Robinson said. "The staff and volunteers of local Catholic Charities agencies throughout the region will be there to bring comfort and hope to their neighbors in need. Please join us in providing critical aid to the immediate and long-term relief efforts."

CCUSA and its member agencies around the country have a long history of rapidly mobilizing following disasters not only to meet the immediate needs but also to provide critical, long-term support to communities as they rebuild. Every year, thanks to the generosity of thousands of concerned donors, the Catholic Charities network responds to roughly 60 disasters, from hurricanes and tornadoes to fires and floods. 

To support those impacted by Hurricane Isaias, please make a gift today.

About Catholic Charities USA    

Founded in 1910, CCUSA is a national membership organization that supports and represents 170 Catholic Charities agencies across the United States and in five territories. Collectively, the Catholic Charities network each year serves more than 16 million vulnerable people, regardless of their faith or background, through food and nutrition programs, affordable housing, disaster relief and a variety of other humanitarian services. To learn more about CCUSA, please visit our website at CatholicCharitiesUSA.org or contact Kevin Brennan, Vice President for Communications, at media@catholiccharitiesusa.org.

data.title: 'I have no children': My aunt gave me $50,000 for a down payment. Now she wants me to leave my home to her two children.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close.'

"I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

Eleven years ago, my aunt gave me $50,000 toward my house, and I'm still grateful. I was 44, newly divorced and buying my first home on my own. I had about $65,000 saved but was short on the down payment for a three-bedroom in a neighborhood I liked. My aunt had money in a savings account earning next to nothing, and she said she'd rather see it go toward a home. She called it a gift and never asked me to sign anything.

The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close. Since then I've put in about $90,000 more: a new roof, kitchen appliances, plumbing work and new windows. The house is worth around $650,000 now, though that isn't cash in my pocket, and I still owe about $180,000. My aunt is 78 and has two adult children, a son,52, and a daughter, 49.

I barely know them. We see each other at Thanksgiving and Christmas; I send cards and birthday texts, and that's about it. My aunt has been a big part of my life. She helped me through the divorce, sat with me when my father was dying and stayed with me for a week after my surgery a few years ago. She has never held the $50,000 over me until now. At dinner last month, she asked me to change my will so the house goes to her two children when I die.

She said it isn't unreasonable and wanted me to consider her offer. She doesn't need the money herself. She just wants her kids to eventually benefit from what she gave me. I told her I'd always understood the money as a gift to me, not an investment in the house or an early inheritance for her children. She had a poker face, but I could tell she did not like my response. I don't want to punish her for being generous. But I'm not comfortable with that request.

I don't want to leave a house worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to two people I barely know. I have no children, and I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about. I haven't thought of the house as a bargaining chip, just as the biggest thing I own. My aunt says I'm being too literal and that family isn't supposed to keep score. Now I feel gaslighted!

Am I being selfish for refusing to leave the house, or a good part of it, to my aunt's children?

Grateful Homeowner

Related: After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan.

Dear Homeowner,

You are not being selfish. You have agency over your own life and finances. You are not being gaslighted. You are feeling pressured.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan and that, to split hairs, is being used as the bargaining chip. You can acknowledge that without agreeing to change your will. If you want to offer something, a modest bequest to her children is a proportionate option. Your aunt may not have meant to have come across so aggressively. Sometimes, people can feel embarrassed in the moment.

If you are uncomfortable about leaving her children any money, don't do it. It's far better to be uncomfortable with your aunt's request and her response to your answer than it is to be uncomfortable with giving money to people you barely know. It's your house - and you can leave it to whom you want to.

What now? Let's assume that $50,000 would be worth $216,000 in 30 years with compounding. You could leave each of her children $108,000, which is more than generous, and reimburses them for the money your aunt gave you out, with interest, assuming that the down payment reduced their inheritance. That's a suggestion, not a request.

You have poured $90,000 into this home to renovate, which has added value; you have worked hard over the last 11 years to pay off the principal and the interest; and you have taken pride in knowing that you have created a home that you can be proud of. Millions of housebuyers get help with a down payment, although it varies by generation.

Homebuyers frequently receive financial help

Four in 10 homeowners received financial help with a down payment on their current home, including nearly 80% of Generation Z homeowners, 56% of millennials and 35% of Generation X (which happens to be your cohort), according to a recent LendingTree survey. The percentage was much lower (12%) for baby boomers.

However, arguably it was easier to buy a house 30 years ago, as the price-to-income ratio has narrowed significantly. Depending on the study, the typical home costs up to seven times the median annual salary today versus just four times the median annual salary 30 years ago. That would explain why fewer baby boomers needed a leg up from parents/family members.

Your aunt definitely overstepped the mark.

Your aunt, for better or for worse, bided her time. You are now in your 50s and never had children of your own, and she has your home in her crosshairs. Yes, she has been a kind and supportive aunt, attending your graduation and helping you get your foot on the property ladder. In many ways, she has been like another mother to you.

If she were your mother, I could see a similar scenario playing out where she would suggest that you support the family cause and leave your house to your brother. But you have no children, and you have already decided to remember your brother in your will, and yet your aunt decided to proffer a version of that request. As an aunt, it doesn't quite land in the same way.

Children often ask the same of their parents

Lest we forget, these pages are rife with adult children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews making similar requests of their elders, asking what will happen to their estate after they're gone, and giving helpful suggestions about what should happen to the estate - which, surprise, surprise! - always seem to favor the one asking the question.

Asking the question is certainly a brazen, if not entirely unusual, state of affairs in families, especially if she considers herself a de facto guardian. However, she definitely overstepped the mark by indicating that leaving the home to her two adult children is the "decent" thing to do. That's a lot more prescriptive than just asking a question.

You don't have to feel ashamed about accepting her gift. Without your aunt's gift, you may never have been able to buy a home or it would have taken you many years. Yes, you are one of the millions of homebuyers receive assistance in the form of a down payment, mortgage payments and/or acting as a guarantor - so her generosity means you are not alone

What do you tell your aunt? You can tell her that you appreciate her help with the down payment, and you will give some thought, but that your estate plans are private. You don't have to answer to anyone. If she persists, you may wish to make it clear that being single and without children does not mean that you have to abide by other people's wishes.

Ultimately, it was a gift, and you can do what you want.

data.description:
Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood Unveils 'Zona de Fuego' Florida's First Fully Integrated Latin Gaming & Entertainment Experience

Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood Unveils 'Zona de Fuego' Florida's First Fully Integrated Latin Gaming & Entertainment Experience

PR Newswire

HOLLYWOOD, Fla., Oct. 9, 2026

A Latin Star-Studded First Bet Celebration

To download photos, click here. To download B-roll, click here.

HOLLYWOOD, Fla., Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood today unveiled Zona de Fuego, Florida's first fully integrated Latin gaming and entertainment experience, during an exclusive preview held as part of its Hispanic Heritage Month celebration, "My Rhythm. My Flavor. ¡Mi Gente!"

The launch builds on the resort's broader commitment to the Latin community, with more than 75 Latin artist performances and Latin-focused events and concerts on property in 2026 alone. Hard Rock Live's lineup includes upcoming performances by Ricky Martin, Dalvin La Melodia, Marcello Hernandez, Grupo Niche and Menudo. The resort also hosts the popular "Noches de Neon" pool parties several times a year and plans to continue the series. Ongoing culinary pop-ups featuring Michelin-starred Latin chefs showcase Latin America's diverse flavors and culinary traditions. Guests can also look forward to Sabores de Las Americas, a Latin food festival taking place Nov. 14.

Joined by several world-renowned Latin music artists, influencers and media personalities for the first bet, President of Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Randy Morton stated, "Zona de Fuego represents an evolution of Seminole Hard Rock Hollywood's multicultural entertainment offerings while strengthening our longstanding connection to the Hispanic community. We created an exciting and welcoming destination that celebrates the energy, diversity, and cultural influence of South Florida's Hispanic community while bringing guests together through gaming, music, food, and shared experiences."

Inspired by Miami's global Latin identity, Zona de Fuego brings the energy, culture and sense of belonging of "Mi Gente" to the casino experience.

CVS Investigation Initiated: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Investigates the Officers and Directors of CVS Health Corporation - CVS

PR Newswire

NEW ORLEANS, Oct. 9, 2026

NEW ORLEANS, Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Former Attorney General of Louisiana, Charles C. Foti, Jr., Esq., a partner at the law firm of Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC ("KSF"), announces that KSF has commenced an investigation into CVS Health Corporation ("CVS" or the "Company") (NYSE: CVS).

On August 2, 2023, the Company announced its financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2023, disclosing that it was revising its diluted earnings-per-share ("EPS") guidance range to $6.53 to $6.75 from $6.90 to $7.12 and that operating income "decreased $1.4 billion, or 30.7%, in the three months ended June 30, 2023 compared to the prior year primarily due to declines in the Health Care Benefits segment[.]"

Thereafter, the Company and certain of its executives were sued in a securities class action lawsuit, charging them with failing to disclose material information during the Class Period in violation of federal securities laws, which remains ongoing.

KSF's investigation is focusing on whether CVS' officers and/or directors breached their fiduciary duties to its shareholders or otherwise violated state or federal laws. 

If you have information that would assist KSF in its investigation, or have been a long-term holder of CVS shares and would like to discuss your legal rights, you may, without obligation or cost to you, call toll-free at 1-833-538-3606 or email KSF Managing Partner Lewis Kahn (lewis.kahn@ksfcounsel.com), or visit https://www.ksfcounsel.com/cases/nyse-cvs/ to learn more.

data.title: Battery X Metals Reports Estimated Driving Range Increase of Approximately 101 Kilometers Following a Single-Electric-Vehicle Performance Evaluation of Next-Generation Patent-Pending Lithium-Ion Battery Rebalancing Technology
data.description:
VANCOUVER, BC / ACCESS Newswire / October 9, 2026 / Battery X Metals Inc. (CSE:BATX)(OTCQB:BATXF)(FSE:5YW0, WKN:A41RJF) ("Battery X Metals" or the "Company") an energy transition resource exploration and technology company, announces the results of a single-electric-vehicle (the "Electric Vehicle") performance evaluation (the "Performance Evaluation") following completion of a lithium-ion battery rebalancing procedure using the Company's next-generation, patent-pending lithium-ion battery rebalancing technology (the "Rebalancing Technology"). The evaluation was conducted by an international arm's length third-party automotive service center, with the results provided by the Company's strategic lithium-ion battery rebalancing hardware and software development partner, Beijing Pengneng Science & Technology Ltd. ("BJPN").

The results disclosed herein demonstrated measurable improvements in estimated driving range together with improvements in battery cell voltage uniformity under the specific operating conditions observed during the Performance Evaluation (the "Results") following completion of a lithium-ion battery rebalancing procedure using the Company's Rebalancing Technology. Estimated driving range values are based on vehicle-reported estimates observed before and after completion of the lithium-ion battery rebalancing procedure during the Performance Evaluation. The Company has not independently verified the Results.

Performance Summary

Under the specific operating conditions observed during the Performance Evaluation, the Electric Vehicle exhibited an estimated driving range increase from approximately 240 kilometers to 341 kilometers per charge, representing an estimated improvement of approximately 101 kilometers, or 42%. According to the third-party evaluation, the Electric Vehicle recovered approximately 85% of its nominal driving range of approximately 401 kilometers, based on the manufacturer's original vehicle range rating, as reported by the third-party automotive service center, demonstrating a meaningful restoration of usable battery performance without replacement of the battery pack.

In addition to the estimated increase in driving range, the Performance Evaluation demonstrated a substantial improvement in battery cell voltage balance. Prior to rebalancing, the battery pack exhibited a maximum cell voltage variance of approximately 41 millivolts. Following completion of the rebalancing procedure and a four-hour stabilization period, cell voltage variance was reduced to approximately 4 millivolts, representing an approximate 90% reduction in voltage deviation across the battery pack. This improvement in voltage uniformity is consistent with the Company's objective of correcting naturally occurring lithium-ion cell imbalance to improve remaining usable battery capacity and reduce the need for premature battery pack replacement.

The rebalancing procedure was completed through direct physical interfacing with the battery pack utilizing the Company's Rebalancing Technology and did not incorporate the Company's standardized vehicle-specific battery interface adaptors currently under development to facilitate integration across multiple electric vehicle platforms for future commercial deployment. The Results reflect performance observed under the specific testing conditions at the time of the Performance Evaluation and may vary depending on electric vehicle platform, battery chemistry, battery condition, operating history, environmental factors and other operating conditions. The Performance Evaluation demonstrated measurable improvements in estimated driving range, substantial restoration of battery cell voltage uniformity, and recovery of approximately 85% of the Electric Vehicle's nominal driving range under the observed Performance Evaluation conditions. These Results form part of the Company's ongoing research and development and real-world performance evaluation program for its Rebalancing Technology.

The Results disclosed herein are based on a single-electric-vehicle performance evaluation conducted under specific operating and testing conditions and may not be representative of performance across all vehicles, battery chemistries, battery conditions or operating environments. Actual results may vary depending on vehicle platform, battery chemistry, battery condition, battery management system operation, load conditions, operating history, driving behavior, environmental conditions and other factors. Accordingly, the Results should not be interpreted as indicative of expected or representative performance across other vehicles or operating environments.

Positioning Within a Growing Battery Lifecycle Opportunity

Global electric vehicle adoption continues to accelerate, with global electric car sales increasing by 20% from 2024 to exceed 20 million vehicles in 2025, accounting for approximately 25% of new vehicle sales worldwide.1 This continued growth is contributing to a rapidly expanding installed base of lithium-ion batteries, many of which are anticipated to transition beyond original manufacturer warranty coverage over the coming years, as most manufacturers offer battery warranties lasting eight years or 100,000 miles, whichever comes first.2 As these vehicles age, battery cell imbalance can reduce usable battery capacity and battery performance, which may contribute to reduced driving range.3

Battery X Metals is developing its patent-pending lithium-ion battery rebalancing platform to address this emerging battery lifecycle opportunity. Rather than replacing battery modules or complete battery packs where battery cell imbalance may be a contributing factor, the Company's technology is designed to restore usable battery performance by correcting cell voltage imbalance, with the objective of improving battery utilization, extending battery service life, and reducing the need for premature battery replacement.

The Results announced herein form part of the Company's ongoing research and development and real-world performance evaluation program for its Rebalancing Technology. The Company intends to continue evaluating the technology across additional battery chemistries and operating conditions as part of its ongoing research and development program.

The Company continues to advance evaluations across additional electric vehicle platforms, battery chemistries, and operating conditions as it progresses toward broader commercialization. Additional evaluations remain ongoing to further assess the performance and applicability of its Rebalancing Technology across a broader range of electric vehicle platforms and operating conditions.

1 IEA, 2 U.S. News, 3 Eneronix

About Battery X Metals Inc.

Battery X Metals (CSE:BATX)(OTCQB:BATXF)(FSE:5YW0, WKN:A41RJF) is an energy transition resource exploration and technology company committed to advancing domestic battery and critical metal resource exploration and developing next-generation proprietary technologies. Taking a diversified, 360° approach to the battery metals industry, the Company focuses on exploration, extending the lifespan of lithium-ion batteries, and the recovery and recycling of battery materials. As global electric vehicle adoption continues to grow and demand for battery lifecycle solutions increases, the Company is advancing its patent-pending lithium-ion battery rebalancing technology, which recovered approximately 99% of capacity lost due to cell imbalance in a technology demonstration conducted in collaboration with the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), with the NRC validating the initial and final state of charge of the cells. data.title: 'I feel like a loser': I check my ETFs every day. They're up one minute, down the next. Should I be worried?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit'

"I haven't made any money in months." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm frustrated with the stock market. One day, my exchange-traded funds go up the next day, and the next day they crash. I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit. I haven't made any money in months. No yield at all. What to do? I feel like a loser. It would have been nice to be able to get a yield. Is anyone else having this experience? What strategies do you suggest for someone who is slowly and gratefully heading toward retirement?

Retail Investor

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I'm never selling': I'm 47 and buy bitcoin with every dollar I earn. Am I crazy?

ADHD is on the rise, which mental-health experts attribute, at least in part, to our personal technology.

Dear Investor,

ETFs are traded throughout the day, but transparency does not equate to volatility.

Yes, they will fluctuate on any given day, week or month, as the news cycle pushes and pulls your stocks three ways from Friday. Yield, for the record, is also different from return; it represents the income generated - like interest and dividends - while return refers to the overall net gain/loss. Technology is all turning us all into checkaholics. We're up there with chocoholics. We want instant gratification, whether it's a boost of dopamine from checking ETFs, or a sugar rush from eating candy. If checking your portfolio is making you anxious rather than helping you make better decisions, STOP checking your accounts.

Focus instead on the long-term trajectory, which historically has tended to rise over decades. Forget about investors making money off microtrades. You don't need to beat those investors. Forget about them; they have nothing to do with you. Checking daily moves in your accounts gives you an inaccurate or, at the very least, incomplete outlook about the stock market's overall health. Here's a reality check. The S&P 500 SPX has risen roughly 14% from January to October, the Nasdaq COMP composite has increased by 18%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA has risen by more than 6% and the Russell 2000 RUT has increased by 13%.

Your anxieties are understandable. The geopolitical backdrop - the war in Iran, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war - has spooked investors and led to fears of a recession, none of which have come to fruition. Occasional check-ins are fine. As you get older, the share of your portfolio invested in stocks typically changes to reflect the time you have to recover from a major correction in the markets (the "sequence of return" risk). That risk is particularly important in the years just before and after retirement: A large market decline early in retirement can damage your portfolio more than a similar decline happening many years later.

Don't miss: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Seeking safety

A few broad strokes: Explore CDs and high-yield savings accounts (HYSAs) for safety, but you may have to sacrifice higher returns. Treasury securities and high-quality bonds can also play a role. You say you are concerned about yield/return. That's understandable. In that case, you should decide how much of your portfolio you want to devote to predictable income, especially if you're upset by the movements in your account, and how much you still need to invest for long-term growth so you can enjoy a comfortable retirement.

There are also psychological and behavioral reasons why incessant checking of your portfolio occurs - and why it can be counterproductive. Loss aversion, a term popularized by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, describes the tendency for people to experience the stress of a financial loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent return on your investment. As a result, you may be inadvertently conditioning yourself to constantly monitor your Robinhood, Vanguard or Fidelity accounts. It's a toxic feedback loop!

Possibly of more interest to you, given your obsessive checking of our own portfolio: Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler developed the concept of "myopic loss aversion," suggesting that the more often you check your portfolios, the more likely you are to notice short-term declines and also react emotionally to them. That's why people sell their stocks in a panic during a market correction and/or go heavy in gold, dive headfirst into bonds and cash vehicles instead, only to regret it later. Don't make a decision on Thursday because of what happened on Wednesday.

Don't miss: 'I'd rather be on a beach in Bali': My husband resents my $8 million net worth. Should I pay for his retirement?

Risk perception

Since you ask about strategies for alleviating risk or the perception of risk: First, take stock of what you actually own and when you'll need the money. If you're overly concerned about short-term movements in your portfolio, you could employ a dollar-cost-averaging strategy, where you divide the amount to be invested in vehicles - be they Treasuries or CDs - into equal-size contributions and invest them over a longer period. Dollar-cost averaging, for example, can make sense when you're investing new money and want to reduce the psychological discomfort of investing a lump sum.

A "bond-tent strategy" involves gradually exposing your portfolio's allocation to bonds in the years leading up to retirement, keeping a higher bond allocation early after retiring and gradually lowering that exposure later. The idea is to create a buffer against needing to sell stocks after a major market decline early, especially early in retirement. It can reduce your sequence-of-returns risk. As long as you have enough money to live on, plus a 12-month emergency fund, it's also worth figuring out how long your retirement savings will have to last and how much you expect to withdraw each year.

A "bond ladder" of individual CDs or bonds, on the other hand, matures at different times and can provide a more predictable income stream while reducing the need to sell investments at a bad time and reducing exposure to interest-rate and stock-market moves. A ladder can be useful if you know roughly when you'll need the money. Whatever you choose, your portfolio should have an age-appropriate mix of stocks and bonds, and cash equivalents. The right mix depends on your spending needs, other sources of income, your time horizon and - yes - your tolerance for risk.

Constant checking creates unnecessary drama. Sometimes, it's better to pick up a good book.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?
